newsitem.title: USA: U.S. rages at new leak to Washington Times.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rages at new leak to Washington Times.

text.p: The U.S. State Department voiced alarm on Wednesday at the latest leak of classified information to the Washington Times newspaper on touchy aspects of relations with China, Pakistan, Russia and other countries.

"If we had a government where every document was available to all you in the press, democracy couldn't function, and we couldn't function," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said. "There would be utter chaos and we would not have an effective foreign policy."

He was commenting on another apparent scoop by Bill Gertz, the Times' defense and national security correspondent who has frequently quoted intelligence reports that have put pressure on President Bill Clinton's foreign policy team.

In his piece on Wednesday, Gertz reported that China had sold more nuclear weapons-related equipment to Pakistan last month in a move likely to increase pressure on Clinton to impose sanctions on Beijing and call into question his China policy.

The report cited what it called a top-secret CIA memorandum dated Sept. 14 as saying senior Chinese officials probably approved the latest alleged sale in breach of a May 11 pledge not to help nuclear facilities operating outside international safeguards.

Burns, referring to "the alleged document" cited by the Times, denied that the U.S. government had concluded that China had broken its May agreement. At his regular briefing, he blasted whomever leaked the memo, calling it a "major" crime with serious national security implications.
The story that irked the State Department on Wednesday was not the first by the Washington Times, whose editorial policy is strongly anti-Clinton, or by Gertz, to upset the Clinton administration.

Vexed by the leaky ship of state, as has been virtually every U.S. president, and apparently feeling stung by Gertz's reports, Clinton, in a memo to cabinet members that leaked in April, called for possible criminal prosecution of leakers.

In June, Burns denounced as "gutless wonders" those who gave Gertz intelligence reports accusing State Department officials of playing down alleged illegal nuclear activities by Egypt, Pakistan and China.

Generally based on documents whose authenticity is not denied by the administration, Gertz's pieces often appear to spring from well-placed officials opposed to Clinton administration efforts to surmount differences with states like China, North Korea and Russia.

Past Gertz scoops have included details from a classified State Department memo of a Clinton conversation with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in which they discussed supporting each other's reelection bids. In March, the White House asked the Justice Department to investigate that leak.

Defense Secretary William Perry called in the FBI after Gertz, in a July 29 Washington Times report, quoted intelligences sources about security lapses at the Saudi complex where 19 Americans were killed in a June bombing.
Gertz, 44, declined to discuss his sources' motives. "Focusing on the leaks is a way to get away from the news value of it," he said in a telephone interview.

U.S. officials have made clear that their target is the leakers, who may have violated their confidentiality oaths and other federal laws, and not the reporter, who is not accused of committing any crime.
Leakers of information meant to embarrass a U.S. administration have a wide range of motives including, at least sometimes, a sense of duty to the truth when they fear it might otherwise be buried.

"But usually they do it to advance their carreers, prove they are in the know or to gain an advantage in a squabble with someone else," said Jody Powell, former President Jimmy Carter's spokesman who now runs a Washington public relations firm.
